title: Composite Crew Oxygen Cylinder Substitution for Weight Saving on the Four-Engine Fleet
abstract: Operator proposal to substitute a lighter composite crew oxygen cylinder on the four-engine fleet, closed without a modification after the weight case failed to survive the certification and logistics assessment.

sections.request: We are running a fleet-wide weight reduction programme on our four-engine aircraft, where every kilogram is worth roughly four hundred euros a year in fuel at our utilisation. One of the items our team identified is the crew oxygen cylinder, which is a steel item and which a supplier has told us is available in a composite version at about eleven kilograms lighter per aircraft. We would like Aeralis to assess whether this cylinder can be substituted, and if so to issue the paperwork. We understand that the bottle is a pressure vessel and that there will be a certification element. We are willing to fund the work and to be the launch operator.
sections.background: The same programme has already delivered a lighter cabin trolley standard and a revised potable water fill policy on this fleet. The cylinder was identified from a supplier catalogue rather than from an Aeralis source, and we have not carried out any installation survey ourselves. Two other operators of the type have expressed interest informally.
sections.expected_outcome: A weight reduction of about eleven kilograms per aircraft with no change to the crew oxygen duration, no new scheduled maintenance task, and an installation that uses the existing mounting.

type_data.business_justification: Eleven kilograms per aircraft at the operator's utilisation is worth roughly four thousand four hundred euros per aircraft per year, and the operator offered to fund the certification work as launch customer.
type_data.closure_note: Closed without a modification. The proposed cylinder is qualified to a service life of fifteen years against the twenty-five year life of the installed steel item, so the substitution converts a life-of-aircraft part into a scheduled replacement and the whole-life cost is negative at the operator's own figures. The mounting cradle would also have to change, which brings the crew rest floor attachment into scope on the four-engine arrangement. The operator was offered the lightweight cradle already released for the twin-engine fleet, which recovers about three kilograms with no certification exposure, and accepted that as a partial answer.
